The chain came out of the water shortly after the sixth bell. At first there was only a line of foam stretching from the mole to the East Quay, then the first link lifted over the parapet, black and dripping and as big as a child's head. Forty men stood at the winches, and not one of them spoke. It was Secondflood, the nineteenth of Neapmoon, and the harbour of North Harbour was being closed.

Oda Brandt stood on the quay and watched the iron settle across the basin. She kept her hands hidden in the sleeves of her coat so that no one would see her counting on her fingers what she did not want to count: the ships outside the entrance, the days until the next spring tide, the men who would soon ask how long this was to last. She did not know. The Council had not said, and she had not asked, because a harbourmaster who asks about the end has already lost the beginning.

"Keep the tension," she called as the winch creaked. "Don't haul it taut. The iron should hang, not snap."

That was not her sentence. She had first heard it thirty years ago, on this very spot, from a man with a crooked hat and a voice like a rusty hinge. Hinrik Salm had had these chains forged when he was harbourmaster and Oda was a girl sitting on a bollard counting gulls. He had never used them. For thirty years they had lain in the chain store, oiled and wrapped in cloth, and on the first day of Strandmoon every year he had had them brought out, only to see that they still shone. "A harbour that cannot close itself is only a wound in the land," he had said. Then he had died, in winter, without a single ship ever having waited at his chain, and Oda had inherited his office, his hat and his sentences.

Footsteps crunched on the gravel behind her. She recognised them without turning round. They were short, precise steps that never hesitated and never hurried.

"The resolution," said Wenke Holm, and held out a scroll. "With the Council's seal. It has been valid since the noon bell. I only didn't bring it earlier because you said you wanted to see the chain first."

"I didn't want to see the chain. I wanted no one to ask me beforehand."

"Then I did it right." The Council clerk was small and wore her grey hair pinned so tightly that it seemed to be holding the rest of her face together. On her right forefinger sat an ink stain that never quite went away. At the Harbour House they called her Quill Wenke, and in twenty years she had neither laughed about it nor complained.

Oda took the scroll and did not break the seal. "What does it say?"

"That the harbour is closed to all traffic until further notice, inbound and outbound alike. That the ferry at the Ferry Jetty is exempt, as long as it does not go beyond the cliff. That you are to run the chain at your own discretion." Wenke looked at the water. "And that the Guild proposed the resolution. That isn't written in it, but everyone in the session heard it."

"The Guild proposes a great deal."

"For three days the Council has followed every proposal."

Oda did not answer. Fog was rising over the basin, as it did every evening when the water grew colder than the air. It crept between the masts of the waiting ships and turned their lanterns into small yellow moons. Out beyond the mole eleven ships lay at anchor. She had counted them once, and then not again, because counting changed nothing.

"The Council listens to the Guild when it comes to maps," she said at last. "It always has. It was never a reason to shut a harbour."

"The Guild says the maps are changing."

"Maps always change. Every tide shifts a sandbank, every winter eats a piece of coast. That is what pilots are for." She pushed the scroll into her coat, among the hands she did not want to show. "I don't believe the stories about the Atlas, Wenke. I believe in iron and in water, and that both do what they have always done."

Wenke Holm was silent for a moment. She had a habit of falling silent after a sentence like that, and Oda had learned that it was neither agreement nor refusal but a noting down in her head.

"I have put it in the minutes that the harbourmaster expressed reservations," the clerk said at last.

"I expressed none."

"Exactly." She turned to go. "It is in the minutes all the same. One can hear it when you say nothing."

The winch clicked one last time. The chain swayed for a heartbeat, then hung still above the water, a black arc from mole to quay, disappearing little by little into the fog. The men took their hands from the cranks. One of them, a broad fellow with a bandaged forehead, stepped up to Oda and asked how long.

"Until I say so," she answered.

He nodded as if that were an answer, and left. Oda stayed a while longer. Down in the basin, where the water almost vanished at ebb, a fish rose, and the rings spread out after it for a long time. Then she went up to the Harbour House, where a single window was burning, and she knew without looking whose pen was scratching there.

***

The net loft lay under the roof of an old warehouse at the western end of the basin, and you reached it by a ladder whose seventh rung was missing. Bela had never replaced it. Whoever knew the ladder stepped over the gap, and whoever did not had no business up there anyway.

Under the beams hung the nets of half the coast, row after row, like curtains of grey hair. Bela sat among them on a stool and mended, as she mended every evening, with a needle of bone and a patience no one would suspect in her who knew her only from the quay. There she was the woman who heard everything and passed nothing on, at least not to the wrong people. Up here she was only a woman with aching fingers.

The hatch banged. Ada came up without skipping the seventh rung, because she did not need to; she simply jumped. She smelled of salt and of the oil she used on the tiller of her pilot boat, and she still wore her oilskins, which had gone stiff in the wet like a board.

"Eleven," she said. "Eleven ships off the mole, and in this current the oldest one's anchor rope will have worked through by morning."

"Then they should take a new rope."

"They may not come in, and they may not go out, and they are to throw out the rope themselves." Ada dropped onto a pile of cork floats. "Twice today I had to row out to tell people I wasn't allowed to bring them in. Twice! The captain of the Gull called me a traitor."

"A traitress."

"He didn't say that."

Bela bit through a thread. She did not look up; she never looked up when Ada was worked up, because she knew it passed faster if you did not watch. The water in the planks of the old warehouse gurgled, the tide was coming in, and with it rose the low grinding of the chain in the basin, a sound like an enormous mouth chewing iron.

"Have you heard?" Ada asked.

"Everyone has heard. The fishermen talk of nothing else. They say the chain was Oda's decision."

"It wasn't."

"I know it wasn't. But she is the one standing at the winch now, so it will have been hers." Bela drew the net taut. "You know people. They never ask who decided something. They ask who carries it out."

Ada was silent, and in that silence you could hear the wind on the roof shingles. She was a broad, strong woman in her early forties, with hands like shovels and a scar across the back of her left hand from a rope she had refused to let go of. She had piloted ships through the sandbars off North Harbour since she was sixteen, and in all those years not one ship she guided had run aground. She rarely spoke of it. Bela sometimes spoke of it for her, on the quay, when someone asked.

"Come out with me tomorrow," Ada said suddenly.

The needle stopped. "The chain."

"The chain won't stop you. I only go as far as the mole, only to the mole. I want to see how the ships lie, and you have better eyes than I do when it comes to currents."

"I have worse eyes than you when it comes to water."

"You're afraid of the water."

"I respect it." Bela stuck the needle into the net. "It's a difference, only you can't see it from outside."

She had always been afraid, as long as Ada had known her, and she had come along every time all the same, on every trip, in every weather. She sat in the bow then, knees drawn up and eyes fixed on one point on the horizon, and did not say a word until she had solid ground under her boots again. Ada had never asked why. She had not needed to. Some things you trusted blindly, and they did not stop being true just because you could not explain them.

"All right," said Bela. "As far as the mole."

"As far as the mole."

"And afterwards you tell me what Oda said on the quay. People on the quay are already telling it."

Ada laughed, short and dark. "She said nothing. She had forty men raise a chain and did not lose a word doing it. It's her way of speaking."

"Then she said a lot."

Outside, the seventh bell struck. The tide went on rising. From the darkness beyond the windows came a call, probably from one of the ships off the mole, and went unanswered. Ada pulled off her boots, set them beside the hatch and stretched her feet out in front of her. Bela went on sewing. They had had these evenings a hundred times without either of them counting them, and they would not do so this time either.

***

On Ebbday, the twentieth of Neapmoon, Oda Brandt counted the barrels at the Salt Market, and this time she looked.

The Council had demanded it. If the harbour stayed closed, they had to know how long the city could live on what lay in its warehouses. So Oda stood among the booths and stalls in a thin morning sun that smelled of fish and wet wool, and had every barrel opened, tapped, weighed and marked with chalk. Two clerks walked behind her keeping lists. Wenke Holm had lent them to her without coming herself. That was her way of showing distrust: she sent a substitute.

"Salt, forty," said one of the clerks. "Dried fish, twelve. That one is salt pork, but it doesn't smell like it."

"It smells like cheese," said Oda.

"It says salt pork on it."

"Then write cheese and salt pork, the one in brackets."

The Salt Market was quieter than usual that morning. The traders had set up their stalls because that was what one did, but they did not shout, and the customers who came whispered. A broad woman in a red headscarf stood behind a heap of grey salt blocks with her arms folded, as if someone had accused her of moving the coast.

"You're counting wrong," she said as Oda stepped up to her stall. "You count what is there. You should count what will be missing."

"I count what the Council ordered me to count."

"Then the Council counts wrong." The woman nudged one of the salt blocks with her foot. "I have this salt from the bay of Graufurth. It comes with the salt fleet, every week, for forty years. Now no ship comes, and what is in my warehouses lasts until the neaptide, if I'm generous."

"The neaptide is in fourteen days."

"I know when it is. I was born on this market." The trader lowered her voice. "And I know what people are saying. That the coast moved north by a boat's length overnight. That the fishermen cast their nets where yesterday there was land."

"Fishermen say a lot."

"My sister is a fisherwoman." The woman looked at her without blinking. "She showed me the place. A wall, with moss, right up to the line of the water, and beyond it nothing, only water, and the wall goes down into the depths. A harbour wall, harbourmaster. Without a harbour."

Oda wanted to answer. She said, "Water has always swallowed walls." That was true, and it still sounded as if she had said it too quickly. Hinrik Salm had once told her that an older city lay beneath the basin of North Harbour, which a storm had dragged down two hundred years ago, and that at neaptide you could sometimes see the tips of its towers if you leaned far enough over the water. She had taken it at the time for a story he used to keep children away from the edge of the quay. Since then she had heard many stories meant to keep children away, and some had later turned out to be warnings.

"I'll write down that you have salt until the neaptide," she said.

"Write down that I have salt until the neaptide and an empty house after."

"I write what I see."

"Then look better."

It was not meant unkindly. That was the worst of it. The trader said it the way you tell someone his coat is open, and then turned to a customer who was asking for half a block. Oda moved on, to the stalls of the fishermen, the ropemakers and the cloth merchants, and everywhere the same thing: a reserved politeness with something waiting behind it.

When the count was finished towards evening, the clerks' book said six hundred and eighty-three barrels, four hundred sacks of flour, seven cartloads of peat and about twelve days of supplies for a city of four thousand people. That was not little and not much. It was exactly the number at which no one could be sure whether the closure was a precaution or a mistake. Oda shut the book and handed it to one of the clerks.

"Take it to the Council clerk," she said. "And tell her I have read it."

"Have you read it?"

"I have counted it. That is the same."

The clerk looked at her as if he would have liked to say something, and then left. Oda stayed a moment longer in the square, among the empty stalls that were slowly being taken down. A gull landed on one of the barrels and regarded her with one eye. From the direction of the harbour came, very quietly, the grinding of the chain, a deep, even note that settled beneath the sounds of the city like a heartbeat you only notice when it falters.

***

What you heard on the quay you never heard all at once. It came in pieces, like water against the piles, and whoever had patience could put something together from the pieces that was very nearly the truth.

Bela had patience. On the evening of Ebbday she sat on an upturned crate in front of the net loft with a net across her knees that she was not mending, and let herself be told. The fishermen came back from the mole with empty hands. They had stood at the chain all through the tide looking at the sky as if it could tell them when they might go out again, and now they stood about in small groups and talked without saying anything.

"Only the Archive still has a light burning," said an old man whom everyone called Cap'n, though he had never owned a ship. "I tell you, the whole quarter lies dark. Not a window in Harbour Lane, not one on the basin. The Council has locked up the oil to make the stores last. But out over the water, there it shines, that glass house, as if someone had shut the stars up inside."

"That's the Keeper," said another. "He never lets his lamps go out. That is his office."

"It was his office. Hasn't he got a visitor just now?"

"Yes, the woman with the coat."

Bela raised her head. She said nothing. She had learned long ago that a sentence you do not interrupt keeps growing, and she wanted to know how far it would grow.

"The Map Reader," said the old man. "That is what she is called, or what they call her. She has been in the city for nearly two weeks and is said to carry a sheet that nobody may see. Her father drew it before he died, and in one place it was supposed to be wet, though it was dry."

"Who says so?"

"The maid from the Tidal Archive. She takes bread over every morning and listens while she's at it."

"And what is the stranger doing there?"

"She sits at the table with the Keeper and looks at maps. No one knows more." The old man spat. "And there is a bird with her, a big white one, circling above the roof and not to be driven off. The young ones say wherever it circles the fog stays away."

That was true. Bela had seen it herself that morning on her way back from the market. Above the glass roof of the Archive a bird had hung motionless, wings wide, and beneath it the air was as clear as in a room without windows, while all around the haze lay over the water like milk. She had looked for a long time. Then she had walked on without telling anyone, because you did not have to tell everything you had seen, and because she did not yet know what it meant.

The old man went on talking, of two men of the Guild who had waited on the steps of the Harbour House with sealed folders under their arms, and of the Council, which now met only behind closed doors. Bela listened and sorted, as she sorted nets, by length and by mesh: what was only rumour, what could be true, what someone had put into the world so that it would be taken for true.

In the end one small, hard piece was left. The Guild had something in mind, and it had to do with the Archive.

She stood up, rolled the net together and climbed the ladder, stepping over the seventh rung. Upstairs a lamp was burning. Ada sat at the table filing a piece of wood that was one day to be an oarlock. She did not look up as Bela came in.

"The light in the Archive," said Bela. "The only one in the city."

"I've seen it. From the water you can't miss it."

"The Keeper is called Iven Rook. You know him."

"I know him the way you know someone you have greeted for twenty years and never spoken to. He has the hands of a man who has handled a lot of paper, and the eyes of someone who would rather handle paper." Ada blew shavings off the wood. "What about him?"

"He has a visitor, a woman who carries a sheet. The Guild has men standing on the steps of the Harbour House, and the Council has nothing but closed doors." Bela sat down. "I don't think this is about the harbour."

"It is always about the harbour."

"No." Bela shook her head. "The chain is only what you can see. It is about what lies in that glass house, and the chain is meant to keep it from coming out. Or someone from going in."

Ada put the wood down. Her face, usually as open as a sail, closed for a moment. "If that's true, then I am on the wrong side of the chain."

"Which side would you be on otherwise?"

"The one I choose myself."

She said it quietly. Bela looked at her and knew that this was the beginning of something Ada had not yet said aloud, and that she would only hear it when Ada herself understood it. Outside, the eighth bell struck. The lamp flickered. On the water lay the ships, eleven dark hulls, and from the Archive, high above the basin, shone the light that no one understood and everyone saw.

***

The Harbour House had only one hall, and for two hundred years it had belonged to the Council. It was long and low and smelled of cold wax. On the end wall hung a map of the basin, painted on leather and darkened by decades of candle smoke, and beneath it stood an oak table with room for nine. On this Lowwater, the twenty-first of Neapmoon, ten sat there.

The tenth was a man of the Guild. He had given no name when he came in, and no one had asked for one. He wore a dark coat with a collar of grey fur and held a sealed folder in front of him on the table, which he did not open. He did not need to open it. It was enough that everyone saw it.

Oda sat at the head of the table, as she had sat there for eleven years, as harbourmaster and as the one who led the Council. At her left lay the Chain Ordinance, a thick book bound in leather that Hinrik Salm had had written thirty years ago. Wenke Holm had fetched it from the house's archive and laid it next to Oda without asking whether she needed it. At her right sat the clerk herself, pen sharpened.

"We have the count before us," said Oda. "Twelve days of supplies, perhaps fourteen if the salt is stretched. The Council will have to decide how long we hold the chain."

"As long as is necessary," said the man of the Guild.

"That is not a number."

"It is the Guild's answer." He spoke calmly and without haste, with the courtesy of someone who has no need to be loud. "In the last few days the Guild has received several reports. The coastlines no longer agree. We have measured them three times. We do not know why, and until we do, no ship can leave the harbour without the risk of running aground on a coast that does not exist."

"The pilots' office says the channel has not changed."

"The pilots' office has no claim to understand maps."

A murmur went round the table. A stout man on the clerk's right, a corn merchant, nodded eagerly. A woman opposite, who sat on the Council for the ropemakers, rubbed her forehead. Oda saw how the session was tipping, like a boat with too much weight on one side, without anyone having made a wrong move.

"For years the Council has left the maps to the Guild," she said. "It has never left the channel. That is the harbour's task."

"The Guild only asks the harbour for patience."

"How much?"

For the first time the man looked at her. In his eyes was something friendly that she hated because it seemed to be honest. "Until we know what is written on the sheet the Map Reader is showing in the Archive. After that the Guild will explain everything."

"What sheet?"

"The last sheet, harbourmaster. It will not be strange to you; it has been the talk of the city for days."

Oda stayed calm. She had never been calm because she felt nothing. She was calm because she knew what happened when she was not. She opened the Chain Ordinance at a place Wenke had marked with a ribbon, and read without raising her voice.

"Paragraph fourteen. The harbourmaster runs the chain at his own discretion. The Council may order it, but not hold it. Whoever holds, bears." She looked up. "Hinrik Salm wrote that. So I bear. I should like to know for what."

"For the safety of the city," said the man.

"Everyone who locks something says that."

"Then perhaps everyone says it because it is true."

It went quiet. Outside a gull screamed, and in the fireplace a log collapsed. Wenke Holm's pen scratched on without faltering. Oda waited to see if anyone at the table would say something, and no one did. That was her answer. She had known it beforehand.

"Then we vote," she said. "Who is in favour of holding the chain until the neaptide?"

Seven hands rose. The corn merchant's first, the ropemaker's hesitantly. Wenke Holm raised none; she raised her pen and wrote. Oda did not count again. She only looked at the man of the Guild, who had not needed his hands and smiled all the same, and she wondered whether he had sat in this hall for the first time that morning or only been visible for the first time.

"The chain stays until the neaptide," she said. "I will run it."

"The Council thanks the harbourmaster," said the man.

"The Council does not thank me. It has loaded onto me something it will not carry itself."

She closed the Chain Ordinance. It sounded like a gate being slammed. Outside, beyond the window, the sky had turned grey, and over the roofs of the city drifted clouds that smelled of rain. The man of the Guild bowed slightly and left, the folder under his arm, without having opened it. The councillors stood up one after another and left the hall like people who have been through a service and are not sure whom the prayers were addressed to.

Only two remained. The clerk gathered her sheets, slowly and in the order in which they had been written. She did not look up as she did so, but Oda knew that she saw her.

***

They walked down the hill to the quay in silence, the harbourmaster and the clerk, through lanes where no light burned and no dog barked. The Council had locked up the oil, and the city had grown used to walking in the dark with a flat hand against the walls.

It was raining now, fine and without wind. Wenke had laid a cloth over the folder holding her notes and carried it close to her body, like someone carrying a child through the night. Oda walked half a step ahead of her. She was used to going first.

"You did not vote for the chain," said the clerk.

"I did not vote against it."

"You called the vote. That is less than for and more than against." Wenke stopped at a corner where a gargoyle spat the rain into a trough. "I'm not asking what you think. I'm asking whether you want me to write the minutes the way the Guild would like them."

Oda stopped too. She looked at the woman who had sat beside her for twenty years and seemed to want nothing, not even the end of the session, and who set down every word in her clear, small hand before it faded.

"What do you mean?"

"There are two ways to write today." Wenke spoke to the gargoyle, not to her. "In one, the Council ordered the chain on the Guild's advice, with seven votes, for the protection of shipping. That is how it will be read later. In the other it says who said what, and that a man whose name nobody knows sat in the hall without giving it, holding a folder he did not open. That would be a very short, very unpleasant record."

"And which have you written?"

"Both."

Oda heard the rain in the gutter. It was strange: she had worked beside this woman for twenty years and never known whether she trusted her or merely valued her punctuality. She had treated the clerk as a part of the house, like the winch or the oak table, something that was there and did its things. It had never occurred to her to ask what Wenke Holm did when no one was looking.

"Hinrik Salm once told me," the clerk went on, "that a record is the only thing a council cannot deny, as long as it is not admitted. I never understood that. Today I believe it."

She had never told him that she had needed him. He had never asked. Between them there had only ever been files, a nod in the morning, a sentence at parting, and when he died she had stood beside the coffin and wondered whether she was now supposed to feel something. He had left her nothing except a habit of keeping a second book that no one saw. She had kept it ever since, page after page, and sometimes she read in it as if she were reading him.

Oda laid her hand on the clerk's arm. It was an unaccustomed gesture, stiff and a little too brief, and she felt through the wet cloth how the woman tensed for a moment and then gave way.

"Write it down as it was," she said. "The second one. And keep it where the Guild cannot reach."

"It lies under the floor of the Harbour House. Under the third board to the left of the fireplace. Hinrik loosened it himself forty years ago."

"I didn't know that."

"That was the point." Wenke smiled for the first time that evening, a very thin, very brief smile. "I always thought you took me for a pen that you dip in the ink. I'm glad I was wrong."

"I took you for a pen," said Oda. "I was wrong. I rely on you."

It was not a great sentence, and it was not said as one. It fell between them into the rain without either of them bending to pick it up. But Oda knew that something had shifted. She knew it the way you know at ebb that the wind has turned: not by any event but by the way the water suddenly strikes the piles differently.

They walked on. At the stairs to the quay their ways parted. The clerk wanted to go back to the Harbour House, where a second book was waiting for her. Oda went down to the chain to check the watch. The rain grew heavier, and on the basin the lights of the waiting ships drifted in rings of yellow and grey, as restless as thoughts that cannot be thought to the end.

Halfway down, Oda stopped once more. She looked back up the hill, where a single window lit up in the Harbour House. In eleven years as harbourmaster, she thought, she had not had one person to whom she could have said what she did not believe. Now she had one. And it was an old, small woman with ink on her finger.

***

On Highwater, the twenty-second of Neapmoon, Ada took Bela out for the first time in days. They went before sunrise in the small pilot boat with the patched sail, and the water in the basin lay so smooth that you could count the stars in it until the oars cut them apart.

Bela sat in the bow. She had drawn her knees up and fixed her gaze on one point at the end of the mole, where in the half-light the chain laid a black band across the water. She did not say a word. Ada rowed calmly and evenly, with short strokes that made hardly a sound, and now and then glanced over her shoulder, not to check the way but to see whether the other woman was still there.

They reached the mole as dawn began. There Ada shipped the oars and let the boat drift. Between chain and quay lay a narrow strip of open water, barely ten paces wide, in which the first light was gathering, a pale, bluish light that seemed to come from the basin itself.

"There," Ada said quietly.

Bela followed her gaze. On the far side of the basin, behind the dark roofs of Harbour Lane, the Tidal Archive rose out of the water, a house of glass on piles in which lamps were still burning. In the half-light it looked like something someone had put there and forgotten. And in front of it, on the road that led from the Harbour House to the Archive gate, a row of dark figures was moving.

"Ten," Ada counted. "Twelve. They walk in step."

"Guild coats."

"And folders." Ada narrowed her eyes. "One goes ahead of them and carries none. He has something in his hand, a sheet or a scroll. He is reading from it."

They could not hear it. The distance was too great, and the water swallowed what was not spoken loudly enough. But they saw the figures halt before the Archive gate, saw the foremost raise the scroll and proclaim something, and saw a shadow move inside the glass house, a single one, upright, which stopped on the threshold and did not come out.

"That is the Keeper," said Bela.

"Yes."

"They are reading something to him."

"They are reading him his sentence." Ada had turned her face away. "You only read out a sentence when you have decided beforehand that no one will object."

The shadow did not move. Behind it, inside the Archive, a second light appeared, smaller and yellower than the lamps, perhaps a candle, and before it an outline, slight, bent forward. Bela thought she could make out a white patch above it, a bird that sat on the gable and watched the scene beneath it with a motionless head.

The boat rocked gently. Somewhere behind them on the quay someone shouted an order, and a winch groaned, but it was not their winch; it was another, on the far shore, where the Guild had its own men.

Oda stood there.

She stood alone at the edge of the quay with her arms folded, and nobody knew for how long. She had seen the Guild's line come down from the Harbour House in the first light, in which she saw everything she did not want to see, and she had done nothing. She could have stopped the men. As harbourmaster she was responsible for every path that ran along the water, and the Chain Ordinance gave her the right to question any group of more than six persons on the quay. She knew the paragraph. She had read it aloud herself only yesterday.

Instead she watched. Not because she wanted to. Because at that moment none of the sentences that occurred to her meant anything: not the Council's, not the Ordinance's, not her own. They were sentences you spoke in a hall where everyone had already decided.

The row of coats vanished into the Archive. The gate closed without a sound. In the glass house three of the lamps went out one after another, as if someone were counting them from inside.

"We're going back," said Ada.

"Yes."

"You're shivering."

"It's cold," said Bela. It was not cold. She looked at the point at the end of the mole without really seeing it, and knew that at this moment she was afraid of something that had nothing to do with the water.

Ada took the oars. The boat turned, and the Archive slid out of their sight, first the glass, then the gable, last the white something that circled above the roof a while longer and then turned away to the north, without a cry. Ada rowed faster than necessary. As they left the channel she looked back once more, to the quay, where a dark coat stood that she knew, arms folded, without moving.

"She could have done something," she said.

"What?"

"Anything."

Bela said nothing. She thought of the grinding of the chain, which she now believed she heard in every stroke of the oars, and of how someone who could do anything sometimes did nothing all the same, because nothing was the only answer left to her.

***

The fisherman came towards noon, in a boat that looked as if it had been built of driftwood and with a sail that was more patches than cloth. His name was Ole, and he was one of those who cannot give up because they have never learned anything else.

He sailed towards the chain in full wind and called from afar: "Open up! I have to get out!"

The men at the winch looked at one another. One of them, the broad one with the bandaged forehead, ran to the quay where Oda stood. She had seen him coming and knew what was about to happen, and she had not managed for one second to prevent it.

"Harbourmaster, Ole is sailing at the chain."

"Then he should turn."

"He isn't turning."

She went down to the mole. By the time she arrived, Ole's boat already lay close before the iron with its sail reefed, and the fisherman stood upright in the stern, fists on his hips. Behind him a pilot boat was rowing up, with two women in it, one sturdy and the other small, clinging to the bow.

"Ole," said Oda.

"I have a family, Brandt." He spoke loudly because he was afraid. "A wife, three children and a mother who no longer gets up. We haven't sold a fish in three days. My nets are wet, and the fish are out there, I can see them from here, standing in shoals the way I've never seen. I only want to go to the cliff and back."

"I may not let you."

"Then you can."

"I may not."

"You are the harbourmaster."

"That is why."

She looked into his face, which was red with wind and rage and something else that she did not want to name. She thought of the scroll she carried in her coat, and of paragraph fourteen. Whoever holds, bears. She was already bearing, she bore eleven ships and four thousand people and a city that had kept itself in the dark for days, and now she was to bear this man too, and his mother who no longer got up.

"Harbourmaster," someone said behind her. It was Ada. She had rowed up to the mole without Oda noticing, and stood in the boat with one hand on the chain. "Let him through."

"Ada."

"You can. One link, a hand's breadth, he is narrowly built. I will take him through the channel myself."

"And then? Then the others come. Ten, twenty. And the Guild says I did not hold the chain."

"The Guild says what it likes."

"The Council hears it." Oda heard her own voice, hard and flat. "I let no one through, Ada. That is the resolution. You know it."

Ada was silent for a moment. Then she said, calmly, with a kindness that was worse than any harshness: "Chain-Mistress."

It was not a title. It was a nickname the fishermen had given her years ago, half in mockery, half in awe, because she was a harbourmaster who loved her chains. She had never liked it and never forbidden it. From Ada's mouth it now sounded like an accusation, and Oda felt the blood rise to her face.

"Take him back," she said. "Bring him ashore. I'll send him fish from the stores, as much as the Council allows. It is little, but it is something."

"Fish from the stores," Ole repeated. "As if I were a beggar."

"As if you were someone I do not want to lose."

That silenced him. He looked at her, for a long time, and then at the chain, and then back at her face, and something in his look changed, not to understanding, but to something like weariness. He gathered his sail. Ada threw him a line and drew him back to the quay, bit by bit, without a word. Bela sat in the bow of the pilot boat through all of it and kept her eyes closed.

When it was over, Oda stood a long time on the mole. The iron hung heavy and dark in the water, and the fish Ole had spoken of were indeed to be seen: silver shadows just beneath the surface, moving in a straight line to the north, as on a road only they could see. She watched them go. She would have liked to know where they were swimming.

The man with the bandaged forehead stepped up beside her. He said nothing; he simply stood there, the way men at a winch stand when they have heard something not meant for them.

"He is right," Oda said at last. "The fish are out there."

"Yes, harbourmaster."

"Have you ever seen fish swim like that?"

"No. But I have never been a man at a chain before, either."

She laughed, briefly, surprised, a dry, unpractised laugh that belonged to the hour and not to her. Then she grew serious again and went up to the Harbour House to tell Wenke Holm that she needed the record of the day. The second one.

***

On Restday, the twenty-third of Neapmoon, nobody in North Harbour worked, and yet the Salt Market was full. The city had come to be read what had not been explained to it.

The Council had decreed it. The Chain Ordinance was to be read out publicly, at the place where for ages things had been read out that concerned everyone: under the salt crane, on a barrel that a beadle had turned upside down. It was Wenke Holm who climbed up. The Council had chosen her because she had the clearest voice, and because nobody else wanted to do it.

She stood up there with the heavy volume in both hands, small and upright in her grey dress, and waited for the quiet. It did not take long. You could hear the gulls on the crane, the creaking of the ropes, somewhere a child that was quickly hushed.

"The Chain Ordinance of the harbour of North Harbour," she read. "Drawn up in the year one hundred and eighty after the Founding, on the order of Harbourmaster Hinrik Salm."

As she read the name she felt her voice grow firmer for one breath. She read out the paragraphs one after another, without emphasis and without haste: that the chain served the protection of the harbour and not its punishment, that it might never be held taut for longer than a month without the Council deciding anew, that every captain whose ship lay at it was entitled to water and bread from the stores of the harbour, and that the harbourmaster who held it answered for every decision herself.

At this point she looked up. She searched the crowd for one face, and found it, at the edge, by the ropemakers' stalls: Oda Brandt, arms folded, without moving. The harbourmaster had promised to come and then had not stood among the people but apart, with her back against a post. It was her way of being present and not part of it.

Wenke read on. The crowd listened, and the longer it listened, the more its silence changed. At first it had been suspicious, then impatient, then it took on something tired and resigned. These were laws that had not been needed for thirty years, and people began to grasp that they might never have had to exist. Whoever agreed to stretch the chain had to be ready to loosen it as well.

"Paragraph nineteen," she concluded. "The chain is to be opened when life on the water demands it."

It stayed quiet for a moment. Then somewhere someone said: "Who decides what life demands?"

It was not a question anyone wanted to answer, and nobody did. Wenke closed the volume. The sound went across the square like a single blow, and afterwards the people began to talk, quietly, all at once. She saw the ropemakers put their heads together and the old man everyone called Cap'n gesturing with both hands. She also saw that Oda was no longer standing by the post.

Ada and Bela met in the afternoon in the net loft. They did not speak about the reading. They had heard it, each in her own part of the crowd, and there was nothing to add. Bela sat at the window looking out at the basin where the eleven ships lay, and Ada paced between the nets with her hands behind her back, like a man composing a speech.

"Tilo was here yesterday," she said at last.

"The ferryman?"

"He came after dusk, when you were already asleep. He didn't knock, he only stood at the ladder and called." Ada stopped. "He wants to go out in fog. Not today, not tomorrow, but soon. He has two people he is to take, and he did not tell me who they are."

Bela turned from the window. She had seen Tilo Krey half a dozen times, a slight, weathered man with a silence that wrapped around him like a coat, and she had always liked him without knowing why. Perhaps because he was the only one at the Ferry Jetty who never talked about the water.

"The ferry is exempt," she said. "As long as it doesn't go beyond the cliff."

"He goes as far as the cliff. No farther. So he says." Ada rubbed the scar on the back of her hand. "But as far as the cliff he has no chart, only memory. There is a current in front of the sandbars that turns at this time of year. If he takes it wrong he'll be aground, in the fog, with passengers. He has asked me for the channel. The exact one, without anyone knowing."

"And you?"

"I haven't said anything."

"You will do it."

"I wanted to know what you think first."

Bela looked at her. The question had something unexpected in it, and she understood how seldom Ada asked it. "I think," she said slowly, "that you have already decided."

"I have." Ada smiled, crooked and tired. "I just didn't want to be the person who does it alone."

"Then you aren't."

Out in the basin the tide struck the chain. It sounded like work, like something that could not be left to rest, not even on Restday. Bela stood up, took a piece of oilcloth from the pile in the corner and began to fold it, with steady hands, as she did everything when she was afraid of something. "When?" she asked.

"Tomorrow evening. At the Ferry Jetty."

"Then you need oilcloth. The paper will get wet."

***

On Firstflood, the twenty-fourth of Neapmoon, shortly after nightfall, Ada knelt on the planks of the Ferry Jetty and drew a coast with a piece of tallow.

It was not a chart of the kind the Guild made, with ink and ruler and golden compass roses. It was a line she set down from memory on the oilcloth Bela had brought, with quick, sure strokes, like someone telling a road he could walk with his eyes shut. Here the sandbank you see at ebb and no longer at flood. There the channel that turns west towards midnight. There, right at the edge, the cliff, and in front of it a spot she circled three times and then marked with a cross.

"Here," she said. "Here you must put the bow into the current, not against it. It feels wrong. You'll be tempted to steer against it. Don't."

Tilo Krey crouched beside her, elbows on his knees, and studied the oilcloth with the attention of a man memorising something he does not want to write down. He was not tall and not broad, but compact in the way only people have who have worked against currents all their lives. Behind him lay his boat at the jetty, a dark, nameless hull with a lantern at the bow that was not yet lit.

"And afterwards?" he asked.

"Afterwards the cliff lies ahead of you. The tower burns, you'll see it even in fog. But the way behind the tower I don't know, and you shouldn't take it."

"I won't take it."

"You've said that three times now."

"Four, if you count the request." He did not smile. He seldom did. But his eyes grew a little brighter, and Bela, who sat at the edge of the jetty with her legs drawn tight against her body, thought for a moment that this man knew something he would tell no one.

She heard the bell. It hung at the end of the jetty from a brass hook, and in fog it rang by itself because the water under the wood moved it. Two notes, one high, one low, and then nothing for a long time. It was a calming sound and yet disquieting, the way a child is calming when it sleeps and disquieting when you do not know what it is dreaming.

"When?" asked Ada.

"Tomorrow. At the first bell after midnight."

"Tomorrow." She rolled the oilcloth together, tightly and with both hands, and handed it to him. "Then keep it. Burn it afterwards."

He tucked it into his shirt. "Thank you, pilot."

"Don't thank me. Just bring them where you mean to bring them."

It was the first time either of them had spoken of "them." Tilo did not answer. He stood and checked the line at the bow as he did before every trip, and Ada watched him with an attention she could not explain to herself.

And then came the horn.

It sounded from far out, from the direction of the mole, a deep, drawn-out note such as no fisherman or pilot used. It was the horn of a freighter, rough and dark, and it repeated after a pause, twice, three times, at even intervals. On the quay a murmur rose. Somewhere a door banged. People came out of the lanes with lanterns in their hands and ran towards the mole.

"That is none of the eleven," said Ada.

"Who then?"

"I don't know. I don't know that horn."

They started to run, all three, Ada in front, Bela behind, Tilo last, with the lantern he lit on the way. When they reached the mole, half the harbour watch was already standing there, and out beyond the chain, in the last light, lay a ship nobody had expected: a broad, deep-laden salt barge with two brown sails hanging torn in the wind. At the bow stood a woman in a weatherproof coat, blowing into a horn almost as long as she was.

When she lowered the horn she shouted across the water as loudly as she could: "The Tern out of Graufurth! Salt for North Harbour, forty barrels! Who opens the chain?"

Nobody answered.

"I am Jorun Estrand!" she called. "I saw the mole from the cliff and thought I was mistaken. For five days I have been sailing in circles because no shore is where it should be. Open up, or I sleep out here!"

Ada stepped up to the chain. She looked at the ship, at the sail, at the woman at the bow standing there like a mast. She had not seen such a ship since the salt fleet stopped coming, and she felt something in her chest loosen, something she had been holding on to for days.

"She can be patient," said someone behind her. It was Oda's voice.

***

Oda stood between the winches, in the light of two torches, and she looked like someone who had been standing there for a long time. Her coat was open, and under it she wore only a shirt, as if she had left the house without thinking. No one had seen her come. It was her way of being everywhere already.

"She can be patient," she repeated. "Until I know what she has loaded."

"Salt!" Jorun Estrand called from outside. "Forty barrels, I said so!"

"I heard it. I want to see it."

"Then come over and look."

Ada let out a sound that was half a laugh. Oda shot her a glance, and she fell silent. The harbourmaster stepped to the edge of the quay, so close to the chain that the damp crept into her boot, and looked out at the ship rocking there like an animal that could not decide whether to flee or stay. The salt barge lay deep in the water, deeper than it should, and the sail hung torn in the shrouds. A ship that had been under way a long time and had not arrived at the right place.

"Five days in circles," said Oda. "One does not hear that often."

"It has never happened before." The captain, a gaunt woman with a grey braid and skin that looked tanned like leather, leaned on the rail. She spoke more quietly now, and the distance only made it plainer how tired she was. "I have sailed the coast down from Graufurth for thirty years. I know every stone, every shoal. Five days ago I sailed out of Graufurth and had the tip of the headland to starboard, as always. I never got past it."

"What do you mean?"

"It wasn't there." She said it simply. "I stood where the headland had to be, and it was water. I sailed north for a while until I saw land, and then south, and everywhere the coast was shifted by a piece, not much, half a mile, a whole one. As if someone had pushed it along with a thumb."

Oda was silent. Behind her, at the edge of the circle of light, stood the clerk. She wore no coat, only the grey dress, and held in both hands the heavy volume of the Chain Ordinance, open at a place Oda did not need to see to know which it was.

"Paragraph nineteen," said Wenke Holm.

"I know it."

"Then you also know that it is not the Council that decides what life demands."

"No," said Oda. "I do."

"I will not open the chain," said Oda. "Not tonight. The Council ordered it until the neaptide, and I do not know what I open when I open it. I only know what the Ordinance says. A ship at the chain is entitled to water and bread."

The captain nodded slowly. She seemed to have expected nothing else.

"Ada," said Oda. "Take the pilot boat. Two barrels of water, a sack of bread, as much as your boat will carry. Wenke, write it down."

"It is already in the minutes," said the clerk. "In the second."

Oda did not smile, but her shoulders sank a little. She watched Ada run to the boat and Bela follow her without anyone asking. She saw Tilo, who stood a moment longer on the mole, his eyes on the salt ship, then turned and disappeared among the lanterns. On the water the light of the pilot boat appeared, small and yellow, and moved towards the Tern.

It was after midnight when the crowd dispersed. The torches burned down one after another, and the men at the winches relieved one another. Oda stayed. She stood on the mole with her coat drawn close around her shoulders and looked at the ship, on which three lamps now burned, and at the chain that hung between her and it. Over the Archive, far behind her, shone the light of the last lamp still burning there.

She did not know when she would open the chain. She only knew that she would, and that this was the one thing she knew for certain that night. The wind turned. From the Ferry Jetty, far away, the bell struck twice, high and low.
